summary: One of two FYI documents of commonly asked questions and answers, written by the IETF User Services Working Group, this one aimed at experienced Internet users. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1207 collects the questions that people running networks asked most often, and the answers that were worked out in practice. It covers statistics, connections to other networks, the Domain Name System, network management, serial lines and routing.

subtitle: The questions experienced operators kept asking, and the answers they had worked out.

tldr.problem: Network operations staff kept asking the same hard questions on mailing lists, and the answers were scattered across those threads and repeated over and over.
tldr.mechanism: Several people read the major mailing lists, picked out the questions that came up most, and published the answers in an FYI memo, grouped by topic and annotated where the editors had to add something.
tldr.outcome: The result is FYI 7, an Informational document that specifies no standard; its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in it.

facts.value: More than 3,300 computers in about 1,400 organizations

today: RFC 1207 is an Informational RFC that specifies no standard. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and its own text says that much of the information in it changes with time and that temporal errors are corrected as the FYI is updated. It stands as a snapshot of what operators were worried about in early 1991.

sections.title: Why This Collection of Answers Exists
sections.content:
RFC 1207 is FYI 7, one of two FYI documents on questions and answers produced by the User Services Working Group of the Internet Engineering Task Force. The stated goal is to document the most commonly asked questions and answers in the Internet, and the memo says it provides information for the Internet community and specifies no standard.

The reason for collecting them is stated plainly. The goal is to codify the Internet lore so that network operations staff, especially those running networks that had just joined the Internet, would have an accurate and up to date set of references to work from. It would also take the redundancy off the electronic mailing lists, so subscribers would not have to read the same queries and answers over and over again.

Several people monitored the major mailing lists over the preceding months and extracted the questions that mattered or came up most often. The answers come from those lists as well, presented loosely grouped by related topic for ease of reading, with the question first and then the answer as it appeared on the list. Sometimes an answer is abridged for space. When a question went unanswered on the list, the editors supply an answer themselves, and these are not marked apart from the others; when they add material that was not in the original answer, it appears under the heading Additional Information. Many questions are in the first person and the answers are addressed to whoever asked, and the phrasing was left alone apart from necessary clarifications, with the correspondents' names removed.

The editors warn that the answers are as correct as the reviewers can make them, but that much of the information changes with time, and that temporal errors will be corrected as the FYI is updated. A subgroup of the working group used three mailing lists to work on the document: quail@ftp.com for discussion and pre-release review, quail-request@ftp.com to join, and quail-box@ftp.com, where questions and answers were forwarded and stored.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo gathers the questions network operators asked most often and the answers that worked in practice. It saves people from asking the same things on mailing lists again and again.

sections.title: The Internet and the Networks Beside It
sections.content:
The first question is where to get traffic statistics for NSFNET, the National Science Foundation Network. Merit/NSFNET Information Services kept statistical data at nis.nsf.net (35.1.1.48) in a stats directory, including packet counts by NSS and byte counts for each type of use such as ftp, smtp and telnet, in files named NSFyy-mm.type. The files were available over anonymous FTP with guest as the password. The answer is careful about what the numbers mean: they cover only traffic that traverses the highest level of the NSFNET, not traffic inside a campus or regional network.

The second question asks how to reach a machine on EARN/BITNET, and the answer explains that several Internet machines act as gateways between the Internet and BITNET, two examples being UICVM.UIC.EDU and CUNYVM.CUNY.EDU. Mail can be addressed to user%nodename.bitnet@uicvm.uic.edu and will be passed from the Internet to BITNET. The same gateways, known as INTERBIT on the BITNET and EARN side, carry mail back the other way, but only from computers that support SMTP mail headers, because many BITNET and EARN computers still do not support SMTP, which is not part of the IBM protocol used.

BITNET and EARN are the two largest of several cooperating networks that use the IBM RSCS/NJE protocol suite, and are not limited to IBM systems. Together with the other cooperating networks they function as a single worldwide network connecting more than 3,300 computers in about 1,400, mostly higher-education, organizations worldwide, and they support electronic mail including mailing lists, sender-initiated file transfer and short interactive messages. BITNET is the United States portion, with more than 550 organizations participating, and EARN is the European Academic Research Network, linking more than 500 institutions in Europe and several surrounding countries.

One date is worth noting: BITNET and CSNET merged organisationally on October 1, 1990, to form CREN, the Corporation for Research and Educational Networking. The two networks remain separate at the operational level, and EARN and the other cooperating networks were not part of that merger. A third question, about ordering documents related to GOSIP, points to PROTOCOLS:GOSIP-ORDER-INFO.TXT on NIC.DDN.MIL and to an appendix to RFC 1169.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says where to find traffic statistics, and how to send mail to the academic networks that ran alongside the Internet. Those networks used different protocols, so gateways did the translation, and only some of their computers could send mail back out.

sections.title: Domain Name System Questions
sections.content:
The longest run of questions concerns the Domain Name System (DNS). The first asks whether there is a DNS query server, and the answer describes a service on host 128.218.1.109 port 5555: connect to it, type a fully qualified domain name, and it replies with an internet address and closes the connection, which the writer describes as a manual nslookup. The answer then says that most users will find it simpler to use a DNS query tool and ask the DNS directly, because that also shows how short names are expanded at the user's own site rather than elsewhere. On a UNIX host with the dig program the answer shows dig x.miskatonic.edu and dig z, and mentions nslookup and similar programs for other systems.

The next question reports frequent BIND failures on VAX and Solbourne machines, traced to TCP domain queries from an IBM NSMAIN nameserver running in cache mode, with UDP queries not causing the problem even though a UDP resolution is usually what is running when the crash happens. Something appears to trash the hash areas, sometimes even during a recursive resolution, and the socket or file descriptor for the TCP connection is occasionally changed to invalid entries, which makes a reply write fail. The answer is that both BIND and the IBM implementation, often called FAL, come in many versions and the older ones are truly bad, so upgrade before investigating further. It adds that BIND has always had a problem with polluting its own database, that the problems have been related to TCP connections and NS resource records with small time-to-live values, and that the style of bug fixing has often been to reduce the problem by 90 per cent rather than eliminate it. The plain conclusion is that the combination of an old BIND and an old IBM server is unpleasant.

Two smaller DNS questions follow. On letter case, the model is that whoever controls a point in the name space is free to choose the case there, until control is handed on, though several implementations get it wrong and IBM implementations often map everything into one case. On glue records, the protocol says an empty additional field is not a problem when the name server's name is not below the cut; putting in glue that is not required can cause problems when the servers named are used for several zones, which the answer calls broken behaviour in BIND, and leaving glue out can cause other BIND problems, usually when the server name is hard to resolve. The advice is to put glue in only when it is required, and not to use aliases when identifying name servers.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the DNS questions are about practical trouble: a name server that crashes, software that changes the case of names, and records that are missing or in the wrong place. The answers are blunt advice to upgrade the software and to fill in only what the rules require.

sections.title: Network Management and Serial Lines
sections.content:
The network management questions start with SNMP authentication. The answer reports that an IETF working group was close to a solution, that nothing had yet reached RFC publication, and that something solid and implementable was expected by October of 1991.

The next question asks how vendors can make their own variables available, and the answer says yes, but that a MIB should be checked first. Two programs are named for the job: mosy-sparc-4.0.3.c, which runs on a Sun-Sparc, and mosy-sun3-3.5, which runs on a Sun-3. Both are retrieved in BINARY mode over anonymous FTP and run over a MIB, for example % mosy mymib.my. A MIB that passes is sent to mib-checker@isi.edu, and if everything is in order the checker arranges for it to be installed in the /share/ftp/mib directory on venera.isi.edu. The answer notes that this processing offers no official endorsement and that submitted documents must not be marked proprietary or confidential. A related question names MOSY in the ISODE 6.0 release as the tool that recognises the 1155 syntax and produces a flat ASCII file.

Another question asks how to decide whether an OCTET STRING should be printed as text or as bytes. The answer is that in general there is no way to tell without knowing something about the object the string came from. Some objects in MIB-II are marked as DisplayString, which has the syntax of OCTET STRING but is restricted to characters from the NVT ASCII character set, and the answer lists them: sysDescr, sysContact, sysName, sysLocation and ifDescr. If arbitrary display is wanted, scan the octets for any that are not printable ASCII; if there is at least one, print the whole string octet by octet in %02x: notation, and if all of them are printable, print the string.

A private MIB object that triggers an action, such as a reset, is handled by defining two values, reset(1) and not-reset(2), with behaviour defined so that reset is the only valid value to set, and any other get or getnext returns not-reset.

The serial line questions correct a common belief: SLIP is designed for asynchronous lines and is not a good fit on synchronous ones, while PPP works on either and is what the answer says to implement. PPP was designed to be useful for many protocols besides IP, and a quotation from UnixWorld of April 1990 records that it had been submitted to the CCITT from the IETF, specifies a standard for encapsulating IP data and other network layer information over point-to-point links, provides ways to test and configure lines and the upper level protocols, and requires only a duplex circuit, dedicated or switched, that can operate in either an asynchronous or synchronous mode and is transparent to the data-link layer frame. The same quotation records PPP as a direct improvement on SLIP, which had neither error correction nor a way to exchange network address. The specification is RFC 1171 and the options specification RFC 1172.

Two practical warnings close the section. SCO's TCP/IP for Xenix supports SLIP, but only with SCO serial drivers, so it will not work with intelligent boards that bring their own drivers. And SunOS 3.5 turns the UDP checksum off, which is legal and works over interfaces such as Ethernet that have link-level checksumming, whereas SLIP performs no checksums, so running NFS over SLIP requires the UDP checksum to be turned on. Without it the result is erratic behaviour such as server not responding: RPC Timed Out.
sections.plainLanguage: The management answers are practical: check a MIB with a tool before submitting it, decide how to print a string by looking at its bytes, and give an action object two values so that reading it is safe. The serial line answers correct a common mistake about SLIP and explain why PPP is the better choice.

sections.title: Routing, Assigned Numbers and Other Practical Questions
sections.content:
Section 9 asks about maximum entropy routing and gets a single pointer: NYU CSD Technical Report 371, Some Comments on Highly Dynamic Network Routing, by Herbert J. Bernstein, May 1988.

Section 10 collects four short answers about protocol and standards implementation. The first asks whether anyone recognises the Ethernet type 80F3, which is not listed in RFC 1010. The answer identifies it as AppleTalk for address resolution, says that Macs directly connected to Ethernet must be present on the network, and explains that these packets are used by the Mac, generally at startup, to determine a valid AppleTalk node number. It adds that RFC 1010 is obsolete and that RFC 1060, the current Assigned Numbers document issued in March 1990, does list 80F3, with the entry AppleTalk AARP.

The second question asks what a high value for Bad proto in netstat output on UNIX machines with Ethernet means, with values in the tens of thousands against a few hundred thousand packets sent and received, and some negative values. The answer says this probably indicates tens of thousands of broadcast packets from some host or hosts on the network, and suggests buying or renting a LAN monitor or installing one of the public-domain packages to find the private protocol that is guilty. It points to RFC 1147, FYI 2, a network management tool catalog.

The third answer, on configuring broadcast addresses when using subnets, says to consult RFC 1122, Requirements for Internet Hosts -- Communication Layer. The fourth explains that .TAR files stand for Tape ARchive: a Unix utility that takes files and directories of files and creates a single large file, originally intended to back up directory trees onto tape, and also used to combine files for easier electronic file transfer.
sections.plainLanguage: The last questions are short lookups. The memo identifies an unfamiliar Ethernet type, explains a puzzling counter in netstat, points to the right RFC for subnets, and says what a .TAR file actually is.

sections.title: Suggested Reading and Security
sections.content:
The memo ends with a reading list for anyone who wants to go further on the Internet and its protocols in general. It includes RFC 1175, the Where to Start bibliography, RFC 1122 and RFC 1123 on requirements for Internet hosts, Doug Comer's textbook, Frey and Adams' !%@:: A Directory of Electronic Mail Addressing and Networks, Ed Krol's Hitchhiker's Guide published as RFC 1118, Tracy LaQuey's Users' Directory of Computer Networks, the companion FYI 4 (RFC 1206) of questions from new users, RFC 1140 on the IAB Official Protocol Standards, John Quarterman's Matrix, RFC 1060 on Assigned Numbers, RFC 1180, the TCP/IP Tutorial, W. Stevens' UNIX Network Programming, and RFC 1147, the network management tool catalog.

The Security Considerations section is one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. The answers deal with availability and configuration rather than with the threats themselves, and the topics of authentication and privacy are not treated here.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo closes with a reading list and one line about security: it says security issues are not discussed. Nothing here treats the threats themselves, only the operational questions people were asking.
